justice: The intersection allocates most visible space to wide motor-vehicle pavement, while pedestrian space is limited to edge crosswalks and narrow roadside margins.
Zebra crossings are present on two sides of the junction, showing some formal provision for non-motorized users, but the overall street design remains strongly vehicle-oriented.
No clearly visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or protected refuge islands can be identified at the crosswalk edges, weakening accessibility for a broad range of users.
The roadside on the right side appears unfinished and dusty with sparse pedestrian infrastructure, suggesting uneven distribution of public-space quality.
safety: Marked zebra crossings improve legibility for crossing movements at the intersection.
The road is very wide and open, which likely encourages higher vehicle speeds and increases crossing exposure for pedestrians.
There is no visible protected bicycle lane, median refuge, or pedestrian barrier separating people from moving traffic through the junction.
Only a few cars are visible, so current traffic volume appears low, but the scale of the carriageway still creates substantial conflict risk.
Large utility poles and an expansive intersection geometry create an auto-dominant environment that can reduce perceived safety for non-drivers.
livability: The streetscape has very limited street trees, seating, storefront activity, or small-scale amenities that would support everyday public life.
Large institutional or industrial-style buildings on the right provide little active frontage at street level, reducing social vibrancy.
Vacant or undeveloped land around the intersection gives the area a sparse and transitional character rather than a lively neighborhood feel.
The broad roadway and lack of visible gathering spaces make the street function primarily as a movement corridor instead of a place for staying.
sustainability: There is no visible dedicated cycling infrastructure or public-transit stop infrastructure to support lower-carbon travel choices.
Tree canopy is extremely sparse, offering little shading, carbon capture, or stormwater benefit.
Large expanses of asphalt dominate the scene, increasing impervious surface area and likely heat accumulation.
Open roadside soil and undeveloped edges are visible, but no clear bioswales, rain gardens, or other green-infrastructure elements can be identified.
aesthetics: The roadway appears relatively clean and uncluttered, giving the scene a neat but austere appearance.
The large power transmission towers and overhead lines dominate the skyline and reduce visual softness.
The building row on the right has a consistent massing and facade language, which adds some visual order.
The lack of greenery, street furniture, and human-scale details makes the overall environment feel plain and monotonous.
comfort: There is almost no visible shade from trees or canopies, so thermal comfort is likely poor in hot or sunny conditions.
No benches, shelters, or resting places are visible near the crossing or along the roadside, reducing physical comfort for people outside vehicles.
The crossing distance across the broad asphalt intersection is long, which can create psychological discomfort for pedestrians and cyclists.
The pavement surface for vehicles appears smooth, which helps driving comfort, but pedestrian waiting areas look minimal and exposed.
Low visible traffic volume may reduce immediate noise stress, yet the oversized open junction still feels harsh and exposed.
walkability: Zebra crossings provide basic crossing opportunities, but they span a very wide roadway with long exposure time.
Continuous, clearly defined sidewalks are not strongly visible, especially along the right-side undeveloped edge, weakening pedestrian route continuity.
There are no visible street trees, benches, or shelters to make walking more pleasant over distance.
The intersection geometry prioritizes vehicle movement, making the walking environment feel secondary rather than inviting.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, protected cycle track, or shared-lane marking is visible anywhere in the intersection.
Cyclists would need to mix directly with motor vehicles across a very wide junction, which lowers cycling safety and comfort.
There is no visible bicycle parking, bike signal, or cycle-specific crossing treatment to support convenient bicycle use.
The large turning radii and expansive asphalt area likely create difficult conflict conditions for cyclists navigating the intersection.
